title: The small one in the middle
theme: He who sends the breath up and down sits small in the middle of the body, and all the gods attend him.

words.gram: n. acc. sg. used as adverb
words.context: Śaṅkara: upward from the heart, «ऊर्ध्वं हृदयात्»
Śaṅkara: «प्राणवृत्तिं वायुम्», the air in its function as prāṇa

words.role: verb of the first pāda; its subject is unstated

words.gram: n. acc. sg. used as adverb

words.context: Śaṅkara: «हृदयपुण्डरीकाकाशे», in the space of the heart-lotus

words.meaning: the dwarf; the one to be worshipped
words.context: Śaṅkara: «वामनं वननीयं सम्भजनीयं», to be loved and served; Raṅgarāmānuja: the same, or small, being the size of the heart-lotus, «हृदयपुण्डरीकपरिमिततया ह्रस्वपरिमाणमित्यर्थः»

words.gram: present participle middle, m. acc. sg.

words.context: Śaṅkara: the senses, «चक्षुरादयः प्राणाः»; Raṅgarāmānuja: those of sattva nature, «सत्त्वप्रकृतयः सर्वेऽपि उपासते»

words.role: main verb of the second line

sandhi.rule: A final m becomes anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
The t of the preverb ud becomes the nasal n before n, P. 8.4.45 (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा).
A final k becomes g before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
After ā the visarga becomes y, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), which is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य), leaving the vowels apart.

sandhi_exceptions.note: unnayati apānam stands unjoined at the pāda boundary in the base (AS); the vishvAsa mūla and Madhva’s text join it (unnayaty apānam), an orthographic difference (corrections.json). Unjoined, the first pāda keeps its eight syllables.

morphology.note: ud-√nī, ‘lead up’, present. Raṅgarāmānuja’s printed mūla has unnamayati, ‘raises’, from ud-√nam, which no witness of this edition reads.
vāmana is ordinarily ‘dwarf, small’; Śaṅkara derives it from √van, ‘love, serve’: ‘the one to be resorted to’. Raṅgarāmānuja gives both senses.
The fourth-class present of √as, ‘throw’ (asyati), distinct from √as, ‘be’ (asti).

translation.literal: [He who] leads the out-breath upward [and] casts the in-breath back — him, the small one seated in the middle, all the gods attend.
translation.readable: He sends the breath upward and drives the downward breath back. He sits in the middle, small and worthy of love, and all the gods wait upon him.

anvaya: [यः] प्राणम् ऊर्ध्वम् उन्नयति अपानम् प्रत्यक् अस्यति [तम्] मध्ये आसीनम् वामनम् विश्वे देवाः उपासते ।
syntax: The first line has two verbs without a stated subject; Śaṅkara supplies the relative yaḥ, ‘he who’, «यः इति वाक्यशेषः», picked up by the accusatives of the second line. The second line is a full sentence: all the gods (subject) attend (upāsate) the small one seated in the middle (objects vāmanam āsīnam).

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the self, which is shown by this as a sign, «आत्मनः स्वरूपाधिगमे लिङ्गमुच्यते». Raṅgarāmānuja: the supreme Self dwelling in the heart of all, «सर्वेषां हृदयगतः परमात्मा».
Śaṅkara: the senses, which bring their perceptions to him as subjects bring tribute to a king, «विश इव राजानम्». Raṅgarāmānuja: all beings of sattva nature.
Small, the size of the heart, or ‘to be loved’ (Śaṅkara, Raṅgarāmānuja); the two senses are not exclusive.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: 16 and 16 syllables, counting unnayati apānam unjoined as the base prints it; joined it would leave the first half-line with 15.

beginner: Breathing goes on without our deciding it: the breath goes out and the breath comes in. The verse asks who does this. Something sits in the middle of the body, in the heart, small and close, and it moves the breath up and down. All the gods attend on it. Śaṅkara explains the gods as the senses: the eye, the ear and the rest keep working and bring what they find to this one, as people bring gifts to a king. Their work is for someone, so that someone must be other than they are. Raṅgarāmānuja reads the one in the middle as the supreme Self in every heart, and the word for small also as ‘worthy of love’.
analogy: Like a conductor in the middle of an orchestra, unseen by the audience, for whom every player keeps time.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Someone leads the breath up and casts the down-breath back; seated in the middle, small, he is attended by all the gods.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: a sign of the self
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The verse gives a sign by which the self is known, «आत्मनः स्वरूपाधिगमे लिङ्गमुच्यते». The senses serve it ceaselessly, bringing their perceptions like subjects bringing tribute, «रूपादिविज्ञानं बलिमुपाहरन्तो विश इव राजानम् उपासते». That for whose sake all the work of breath and senses goes on is other than they, «यदर्था यत्प्रयुक्ताश्च सर्वे वायुकरणव्यापाराः, सोऽन्यः सिद्ध इति वाक्यार्थः».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the Lord in the heart
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The one who moves the breaths is the supreme Self in the heart of all, «सर्वेषां हृदयगतः परमात्मा», seated in the heart-lotus, «हृदयपुण्डरीकमध्ये आसीनं वामनम्», and served by all beings of sattva nature.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: prāṇa and apāna here are the two movements of breath, upward and downward. The verse gives no subject to the first line; Śaṅkara supplies the relative ‘he who’, which the accusatives of the second line take up.

advaita.text: The self is known as other than the breaths and senses that work for it, «सोऽन्यः सिद्ध इति वाक्यार्थः».

visistadvaita.text: The mover of the breaths is the supreme Self in every heart, «सर्वेषां हृदयगतः परमात्मा».

schools.disagreement: Both read the one in the middle as the self that the breaths and senses serve: for Śaṅkara, the self known as other than them; for Raṅgarāmānuja, the supreme Self dwelling in the heart. Madhva’s bhāṣya comments once on 2.2.3–5, on breath upheld by Viṣṇu; that comment is quoted at 2.2.5.

parallels.note: The Praśna says that breath is born from the self, as the Kaṭha says breath is moved by it.

contemporary.text: Most of what keeps us alive happens without our choosing — breath, heartbeat, the work of the senses. The verse turns that ordinary fact into a question about who all this activity is for. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Can you notice your breath going on without your deciding it?
reflect.deeper: Why does Śaṅkara think that service by the senses proves there is someone other than them?
reflect.practice: Sit for two minutes and simply watch the breath rise and fall, without changing it.

flags.note: The subject of the first line is unstated; the gods are the senses (Śaṅkara) or beings of sattva nature (Raṅgarāmānuja).
